subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: B3.1 — Gas exchange & B3.2 — Transport (Apr–May unit)

cards.front: Why do large organisms need specialized gas exchange surfaces and transport systems?
cards.back: As size increases, surface area-to-volume ratio falls → diffusion alone can't reach inner cells → specialized surfaces + a circulatory system.

cards.front: Four properties of efficient gas exchange surfaces
cards.back: Thin (short diffusion path), moist (gases dissolve), large surface area, dense blood supply/ventilation maintaining the gradient.
Huge total surface area (millions of alveoli), one-cell-thick walls, moist surface, dense capillary network — steep gradients on both sides.

cards.front: Type I vs Type II pneumocytes
cards.back: Type I: extremely thin flattened cells for gas exchange (~95% of surface). Type II: secrete surfactant, preventing alveolar collapse.
Lipid-protein secretion reducing surface tension in the alveoli — stops them collapsing on exhalation.
Diaphragm contracts (flattens) + external intercostals lift the ribs → volume increases → pressure drops below atmospheric → air flows in. Exhalation at rest is passive recoil.

cards.front: Leaf gas exchange — where and what?
cards.back: Stomata: pores opened/closed by guard cells. CO₂ diffuses in for photosynthesis; O₂ and water vapour diffuse out — the photosynthesis/transpiration trade-off.
Pulmonary circuit (right heart → lungs → left heart) + systemic circuit (left heart → body). Blood passes the heart twice per circuit → full pressure to both lungs and body.
The pacemaker — muscle cells in the right atrium that initiate each heartbeat. Impulse → atria contract → AV node → Purkinje fibres → ventricles.

cards.front: Aorta vs pulmonary artery — which blood?
cards.back: Aorta: oxygenated blood to the body. Pulmonary artery: the exception among arteries — carries DEoxygenated blood to the lungs. Pulmonary vein: the vein carrying oxygenated blood.
Arteries: thick muscular/elastic walls for high pressure + elastic recoil. Veins: thinner, lower pressure, valves to prevent backflow.
One cell thick (short diffusion distance), permeable walls, enormous total surface area from branching, narrow — red cells squeeze close to the wall.
Xylem: dead hollow tubes, water + minerals UP only (transpiration pull). Phloem: living sieve tubes, sucrose both directions (translocation).
Water vapour loss from leaves through open stomata — driven by light, heat, wind and low humidity; the engine of the transpiration stream.
Evaporation pulls the water column; cohesion (H-bonds) holds it together; adhesion to the walls supports it; root pressure pushes from below.
Sucrose actively loaded at SOURCES (mature leaves) → high pressure → flows to SINKS (roots, fruits, growing tips). Direction varies with the season.

cards.front: Guard cells — when do stomata open?
cards.back: Light → potassium ions pumped in → osmotic water uptake → turgid guard cells bow apart. Water stress or darkness closes them.
Volume/pressure changes during breathing: identify inhalation (volume up, pressure down) vs exhalation, and explain with the diaphragm/intercostals.
Sequence the structures without deep detail: air → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli → capillaries.
